title: Feast food
hook: feasts with food: pancakes, fish, cakes
tomorrow: why would anyone walk to the same place every single year?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: your saint's day, a feast with a friend's name on it. And a feast, sooner or later, needs a table.
screen: `YOUR SAINT'S DAY.` → `A FEAST NEEDS A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Some smells are a calendar. Masa steaming in corn husks in December. Pancakes on a Tuesday in February. Fish on a Friday in Lent. Before anyone says a word, your nose knows what day it is. A feast day tastes like that: like a particular kitchen, on a particular day, with particular people. And the Bible has a line that asks you to taste first and understand after.
screen: `SOME SMELLS ARE A CALENDAR.` → `YOUR NOSE KNOWS THE DAY.` → `TASTE FIRST.`

segments.voice: It's in the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet." Taste comes before see. Then there's a scene in the book of Nehemiah. The law is read aloud to the people after the exile, and they weep. And they're told: don't be sad. Go, eat rich food, drink something sweet, and send portions to those who have nothing ready, because this day is holy. One to tell a friend: in that scene, the holy day isn't finished until the ones with an empty table get a plate. Catholic kitchens kept that rhythm. Tradition says Shrove Tuesday pancakes used up the eggs and butter before Lent's fast. Fish on Lent's Fridays is fasting food, the quiet that makes the feast taste better when it comes. King cake at Epiphany, tamales at Christmas in some families, bread braided for Easter. And Jesus's first sign in John's Gospel happens at a wedding feast in Cana, where the steward tastes the new wine and tells the groom, "thou hast kept the good wine until now." A feast in this tradition isn't a break from faith. It's one of the places faith happens, with the mouth.
screen: `O TASTE, AND SEE.` · `SEND PORTIONS TO THE EMPTY TABLE.` · `PANCAKES, FISH, KING CAKE.` · `THE GOOD WINE UNTIL NOW.` · then, large: `FAITH YOU CAN TASTE.`

segments.voice: Take one small thing to eat or drink: a piece of bread, a bit of fruit, a sip of something warm. Smell it first, with your eyes open. Then taste it slowly, the way you would a dish someone spent all day making. If you pray, you can say, between bites, O taste, and see.
Feast food. The dishes that mark holy days: pancakes before Lent, fish on its Fridays, cakes and tamales when the feast comes. Today's word.
Your line: faith you can taste, with a plate saved for the empty table. Back tomorrow.

chat.meaning: In this tradition a feast is faith you can taste: O taste, and see, and a holy day that sends portions to those with nothing ready.

Masa.meaning: Spanish: corn dough, used for tamales

Lent.meaning: the season of fasting and prayer before Easter

Nehemiah.meaning: a Jewish leader who helped rebuild Jerusalem after the exile

Shrove Tuesday.meaning: the day before Lent begins, known for pancakes

Epiphany.meaning: the feast of the magi's visit to the child Jesus

Cana.meaning: the village wedding where Jesus turned water into wine

sources.ref: Code of Canon Law (1983), canons 1250–1251 (Fridays of Lent; abstinence from meat)

notes: Psalm 33:9 and John 2:10 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording.
Nehemiah 8:9–12 paraphrased (in the Douay-Rheims, 2 Esdras 8; the speaker is Nehemias/Esdras with the Levites). 'after the exile' is the setting of the book. Confirm.
Shrove Tuesday pancakes using up eggs and butter: voiced as 'tradition says'. King cake, tamales and braided Easter bread are named as customs 'in some families', without claims about how widespread.
Fish on Lent's Fridays: canon 1251 abstinence from meat; fish described as fasting food. Confirm framing.
